questions.question: Define the terms hydrocarbon, functional group and homologous series, and use pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane to explain what structural isomers are.
questions.expected_answer: A hydrocarbon is a compound containing only carbon and hydrogen atoms. A functional group is a bond, an atom or a group of atoms that determines the physical and chemical properties of a group of organic compounds — for example the carbon-carbon double bond in alkenes or the hydroxyl (OH) group in alcohols. A homologous series is a series of organic compounds that can be described by the same general formula, in which each member differs from the previous one by a CH₂ unit — the alkanes CnH2n+2 are the standard example. Structural isomers are molecules with the same molecular formula but different structural formulae. Pentane and 2,2-dimethylpropane are both C₅H₁₂, but pentane is an unbranched five-carbon chain while 2,2-dimethylpropane has a central carbon bonded to four other carbons. The same atoms are connected in different arrangements, so they are structural isomers — specifically chain isomers — and they are genuinely different compounds with different names and different boiling points.

questions.question: A compound has a five-carbon chain with a double bond between carbon 2 and carbon 3, and a methyl group on carbon 4 (numbering from the end nearest the double bond). Give its IUPAC name, explain the numbering direction, and explain what the locant of a double bond refers to.
questions.expected_answer: The name is 4-methylpent-2-ene. The longest chain containing the functional group is five carbons, giving the root pent; the double bond makes it an alkene, suffix -ene. Because the double bond is the functional group, the chain must be numbered from the end that gives it the lowest possible locant: from the near end the double bond starts at carbon 2 and the methyl group falls on carbon 4. Numbering from the far end would put the first carbon of the double bond at position 3 and the methyl at position 2 — but the functional group outranks substituents in numbering, so pent-2-ene beats pent-3-ene and the near-end numbering is correct. The locant quoted for a double bond always refers to the FIRST (lower-numbered) carbon of the pair of carbons that the double bond joins — pent-2-ene means the double bond lies between carbons 2 and 3.

questions.question: Butanal and butanone both have the molecular formula C₄H₈O. Describe each structure in words, classify the isomerism, and explain why a molecular formula on its own can never fully identify an organic compound.
questions.expected_answer: Butanal is an aldehyde: a four-carbon chain whose end carbon (carbon 1) carries the carbonyl group — a carbon double-bonded to an oxygen — and is also bonded to a hydrogen, with the remaining carbons carrying their full complement of hydrogens. Butanone is a ketone: a four-carbon chain in which carbon 2, an inner carbon, carries the carbonyl group and is bonded to a carbon on each side. They are functional isomers: compounds with the same molecular formula that belong to different homologous series. This is exactly why a molecular formula can never identify a compound on its own — C₄H₈O only counts atoms and says nothing about which atom is bonded to which. Properties are set by structure, and above all by the functional group, so two compounds sharing one formula can have different families, names, suffixes, boiling points and reactions. Only a structural or condensed formula, which records the bonding arrangement, pins the compound down uniquely.
